coronation: The Coronation is usually linked to Edward VII, whose coronation in 1902 was postponed at two days' notice when the king needed emergency surgery, though who first mixed a drink in its honour is not on record. Its most familiar form, dry vermouth and sherry with dashes of maraschino and orange bitters, survives through Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930, which lists it as the Coronation No. 1.
turf-cocktail: The Turf is older than its settled recipe: a Turf Club cocktail of Old Tom gin and sweet vermouth was already in print in the 1880s, very close to the Martinez. The drier formula arrived in 1900, when the New York bartender Harry Johnson added a Turf Cocktail of Plymouth gin, dry vermouth, maraschino, absinthe and orange bitters to the revised edition of his Bartenders' Manual. No one recorded the reason for the name, and bar books long disagreed over where the Turf ended and the Tuxedo began.
income-tax: The Income Tax is a Bronx with a dash of Angostura, and it appears in Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 as dry gin, French and Italian vermouth, the juice of a quarter orange and bitters. Who first mixed it, and which country's income tax it was named after, is not recorded.
bobby-burns: Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 gives the Bobby Burns as Scotch and Italian vermouth with a few dashes of Bénédictine, and singles it out among whisky cocktails. The old Waldorf-Astoria in New York had served a Robert Burns of Scotch, Italian vermouth, orange bitters and absinthe, and its chronicler Albert Stevens Crockett thought it more likely named for a cigar salesman who drank at the bar than for the poet; Robert Burns was also a cigar brand of the day. Bar books have spelled the name several ways since.
affinity: The Affinity, equal parts Scotch, sweet and dry vermouth with a dash of bitters, is an American drink of the early twentieth century that Harry Craddock included in The Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930. Its creator is unrecorded, and so is the reason for its name.
old-pal: Harry MacElhone printed the Old Pal in the 1922 edition of his ABC of Mixing Cocktails and credited it to William 'Sparrow' Robertson, sporting editor of the New York Herald's Paris edition and a regular at Harry's New York Bar. Robertson is said to have greeted everyone as 'old pal', and the name went to the drink. MacElhone's recipe used Canadian whisky with dry vermouth and Campari; the drink surfaced again in his Barflies and Cocktails of 1927, and modern versions usually use rye.
scofflaw: In January 1924 a contest backed by the Prohibitionist Delcevare King chose 'scofflaw' as the new word for anyone who drank illegally. Within weeks the Chicago Tribune reported that Jock, a bartender at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, had answered with a Scofflaw cocktail of rye, dry vermouth, lemon and grenadine. It was a Paris joke at the expense of Prohibition, mixed where the law could not reach, and the word stayed in the language long after the law it described was repealed.
diamondback: Ted Saucier printed the Diamondback in Bottoms Up, his 1951 collection of hotel and bar drinks, crediting it to the Diamondback Lounge of the Lord Baltimore Hotel in Baltimore: rye and applejack with a measure of yellow Chartreuse. The bartender who created it was never named, and how long the lounge had been pouring it before the book appeared is not recorded.
de-la-louisiane: Stanley Clisby Arthur recorded this drink in 1937 in Famous New Orleans Drinks and How to Mix 'Em, as the house cocktail of Restaurant de la Louisiane on Iberville Street, a Creole dining room that had been open since 1881. Arthur's recipe set rye against sweet vermouth and Bénédictine with dashes of absinthe and Peychaud's bitters, which makes it a close relative of the Vieux Carré of the same era. New Orleans bartenders revived it during the cocktail renaissance, often under the shorter name La Louisiane.
fancy-free: The Fancy Free appears in Crosby Gaige's Cocktail Guide and Ladies' Companion of 1941, a simple build of whiskey with dashes of maraschino and both orange and Angostura bitters, the liqueur doing the job that sugar does in an Old Fashioned. Gaige was a Broadway producer and noted gourmet, and the drink belongs to the same family as the nineteenth-century Improved Whiskey Cocktail. Who first mixed it is not recorded.
improved-whiskey-cocktail: In the 1876 edition of his Bar-Tender's Guide, Jerry Thomas added 'improved' versions of the brandy, gin and whiskey cocktails, upgrading the old formula of spirit, sugar and bitters with dashes of maraschino and absinthe. Improved was a recognised recipe category rather than a boast, and the name stuck. The style faded as the Old Fashioned and the Manhattan took over the bar, and it returned to menus during the modern cocktail revival.
morning-glory-fizz: Harry Johnson printed the Morning Glory Fizz in his Bartenders' Manual of 1882, made with Scotch, lemon and lime juice, sugar, egg white and a few dashes of absinthe, topped with soda. Like the other fizzes of its day it was served the moment it was made, before the soda went flat. Whether Johnson invented it or simply recorded it is not known.
sloe-gin-fizz: Sloe gin began as an English country liqueur, made by steeping blackthorn sloes in gin with sugar, traditionally after the first frost, which makes it strictly a liqueur rather than a gin. American bartenders built it into the gin fizz template with lemon, sugar and soda before Prohibition, and no one has claimed the invention.
chicago-fizz: The Chicago Fizz is a pre-Prohibition fizz of rum and port shaken with lemon and egg white and lengthened with soda, and its inventor and the reason for its name are not on record.
whiskey-smash: Jerry Thomas put the smash into print in 1862, in How to Mix Drinks, describing it as simply a julep on a small plan: spirit, sugar and mint over shaved ice in a smaller glass, with brandy, gin and whiskey versions. The lemon that defines the modern Whiskey Smash came much later, and the version most bartenders now follow, with lemon wedges muddled alongside the mint, is widely credited to Dale DeGroff. The smash has stayed a summer drink, built from whatever is fresh.
brandy-flip: The flip was a tavern drink long before it was a cocktail: in seventeenth-century England and colonial America it meant beer, rum and sugar, frothed by plunging a red-hot iron called a loggerhead, or flip dog, into the mug. By the time Jerry Thomas published How to Mix Drinks in 1862, egg had largely replaced the beer and the iron, and his book gives hot and cold flips built on brandy, gin, rum and whiskey. The brandy version, finished with grated nutmeg, is the form that survived into the modern bar.
coffee-cocktail: Jerry Thomas published the Coffee Cocktail in the 1887 edition of his Bar-Tender's Guide, and then felt obliged to explain the name: the drink contains neither coffee nor bitters, he wrote, but looks like coffee when properly made. The look comes from shaking port and brandy with a whole egg and sugar until the foam turns a milky brown. It is a close cousin of the flips of the same era, and it remains one of the stranger names in the classic canon.
bourbon-milk-punch: Milk punch is one of the oldest mixed drinks in the English-speaking world, and its colonial versions were often clarified, the milk curdled and strained out. The simpler style made with whole milk, sugar and spirit became a Southern holiday and brunch tradition, and in New Orleans it settled into the menus of the old Creole restaurants, where brandy and bourbon versions are served under a dusting of nutmeg. Brennan's on Royal Street is the restaurant most associated with it, though no one claims to have invented it.
presbyterian: The Presbyterian is a whisky highball split between ginger ale and soda water, a long-standing standby of American bars whose creator, date and name have never been explained.
mamie-taylor: Rochester, New York, 1899: the story goes that the singer and actress Mayme Taylor, back from a sail on Lake Ontario at Ontario Beach, asked for a claret lemonade, and the bartender, usually named as Bill Sterritt, gave her Scotch with lime and ginger ale instead. Newspapers spelled her name Mamie, and around 1900 the drink became a national craze. The Moscow Mule later followed the same template with vodka, and the Mamie Taylor faded.
nevada: The Nevada is a short rum sour sharpened with grapefruit and lime and seasoned with Angostura, usually grouped with the Cuban rum drinks of the Daiquiri family, though its creator and the reason for its name are unrecorded.
hotel-nacional: The Hotel Nacional de Cuba opened in Havana in 1930, during American Prohibition, and drew leading American bartenders of the day. Its flagship drink, the Hotel Nacional Special of rum, pineapple, apricot brandy and lime, has been credited to three of them, Wil P. Taylor, Eddie Woelke and Fred Kaufman, and Charles H. Baker's Gentleman's Companion of 1939 gave the honour to Taylor. The hotel later hosted the 1946 mob gathering that inspired a scene in The Godfather Part II.
air-mail: The Air Mail first appeared in a Bacardi advertising brochure in the early 1930s, when airmail was still the fastest way to send word across borders: rum, citrus and honey topped with sparkling wine. W. C. Whitfield printed it in Just Cocktails in 1939 and Here's How in 1941, Esquire's Handbook for Hosts of 1949 described it as a cross between the French 75 and the Honey Bee, and the PDT Cocktail Book brought it back to prominence in 2011.
gibson: The Gibson's namesake is still argued over. A relative of the San Francisco businessman Walter D. K. Gibson said he devised it at the Bohemian Club in the 1890s, the account now usually thought more likely, while another story credits the illustrator Charles Dana Gibson, creator of the Gibson Girl, who is said to have challenged a bartender at the Players club in New York to improve on the Martini. The first known recipe garnished with an onion appears in William Boothby's The World's Drinks and How to Mix Them of 1908.
dirty-martini: The Dirty Martini, a Martini sharpened with a splash of olive brine, has no recorded creator or date, and the popular claim that Franklin Roosevelt made it fashionable at the White House rests on anecdote rather than record.
black-manhattan: Todd Smith created the Black Manhattan at Bourbon & Branch in San Francisco in 2005, replacing the sweet vermouth of the classic with Averna, the Sicilian amaro. The swap was part of a wider move by bartenders of the time to treat amari as cocktail ingredients rather than after-dinner sippers, and the drink travelled quickly from San Francisco to bars across the United States, where it did much to introduce Averna to American drinkers.
bensonhurst: Chad Solomon created the Bensonhurst in 2006 at Milk & Honey in New York, adding to a run of rye drinks named for Brooklyn neighbourhoods that began with Vincenzo Errico's Red Hook, each a riff on the Brooklyn cocktail. Solomon's version stirs rye with dry vermouth, maraschino and a little Cynar, and the series went on to include the Greenpoint and others.
rosita: The Rosita has no recorded creator, and the recipe most bartenders follow is the one Gary Regan printed in The Bartender's Bible in 1991: tequila stirred with sweet and dry vermouth, Campari and a dash of bitters. It became one of the most familiar tequila relatives of the Negroni.
kingston-negroni: Joaquín Simó created the Kingston Negroni at Death & Co in New York in 2009, around the time the importer Eric Seed brought Smith & Cross, a navy-strength Jamaican rum, to the American market. As the story is usually told, Simó tested the rum by building an equal-parts Negroni with it on the spot, and the result helped persuade bartenders that funky Jamaican rum belonged in stirred drinks.
mezcal-negroni: The Mezcal Negroni swaps the gin of the Florentine original for the smoky agave spirit of Oaxaca, a variation that spread through American cocktail bars without any single bar or bartender claiming the first.
jet-pilot: The Jet Pilot was created around 1958 at the Luau, Steve Crane's Polynesian restaurant in Beverly Hills, as a remake of Don the Beachcomber's Test Pilot. Crane's version dropped the Cointreau and added grapefruit juice and cinnamon syrup, while keeping the Beachcomber habits of mixed rums, falernum, a few drops of absinthe and a dash of Angostura. Of the many copies the Test Pilot inspired, it is the one that lasted, helped by its long run on the menu at the Mai-Kai in Fort Lauderdale.
test-pilot: Don the Beachcomber created the Test Pilot at his Hollywood bar around 1941, built on Jamaican and Puerto Rican rums with Cointreau, falernum, lime, a few drops of absinthe and a dash of Angostura. Like all of Donn Beach's recipes it was guarded with coded bottles and pre-mixed syrups, yet it became one of the most copied drinks of the tiki era, inspiring the Jet Pilot among others. The recipe followed today is the one documented by the tiki historian Jeff Berry.
doctor-funk: The travel writer Frederick O'Brien described the Doctor Funk in White Shadows in the South Seas in 1919, naming it for Bernard Funk, a German physician in Samoa credited with the mix of absinthe, grenadine, lime juice and soda water. Funk had attended Robert Louis Stevenson in Samoa, where the writer died in 1894, and his drink became known across the South Pacific. O'Brien's book made it famous in America, and both Don the Beachcomber and Trader Vic later created their own versions.
cobras-fang: The Cobra's Fang is one of Don the Beachcomber's early recipes, usually dated to around 1937, when his Hollywood bar was turning rum, citrus and spice into what became tiki. It sets a high-proof Demerara rum against orange and lime, falernum, a dash of absinthe and Angostura, and like most of Donn Beach's drinks it was guarded by coded recipes. Its modern form owes much to the research of the tiki historian Jeff Berry.
missionarys-downfall: The Missionary's Downfall is a Don the Beachcomber recipe from his Hollywood bar, and it is essentially an amplified Daiquiri: light rum, lime and honey blended with fresh pineapple, peach brandy and a generous handful of mint into a pale green frappé. The origin of the name is not recorded.
nui-nui: The Nui Nui comes from Don the Beachcomber's Hollywood bar. Donn Beach mixed his spice syrups in advance and labelled them only with numbers, so that even his own bartenders could not copy his drinks, and this one depended on a blend of vanilla and allspice listed simply as Don's Spices No. 2. The codes were cracked decades later by the tiki historian Jeff Berry, whose research with former Beachcomber staff brought recipes like this back to bars.
pearl-diver: Donn Beach created the Pearl Diver at his Hollywood bar in the 1930s, built around gardenia mix, a spiced blend of butter and honey that emulsifies into the rums and juices. The formula was effectively lost until the tiki historian Jeff Berry recovered it from the notebook of a former Beachcomber bartender, Dick Santiago, and published it in Sippin' Safari in 2007.
royal-hawaiian: The Royal Hawaiian is a gin drink with pineapple, lemon and orgeat named for the pink Royal Hawaiian hotel on Waikiki Beach, one of the few tiki-era drinks built on gin, and accounts of who first mixed it differ.
halekulani: The Halekulani is the house cocktail of the Halekulani hotel on Waikiki, whose oceanfront bar, House Without a Key, takes its name from Earl Derr Biggers's first Charlie Chan novel, which the author is said to have conceived during a stay at the hotel.
beachcomber: The Beachcomber appears in Trader Vic's Bartender's Guide of 1947, a dry Daiquiri variation with triple sec and a touch of maraschino. Its name is generally taken as a salute to Don the Beachcomber, the Hollywood bar that Ernest Raymond Beaumont Gantt opened in the early 1930s and that launched the tiki craze, though which of the rival tiki houses first mixed it is unclear. Gantt identified so completely with his bar that he legally changed his name to Donn Beach.
chief-lapu-lapu: The Chief Lapu Lapu is a mid-century tiki punch with no recorded creator, named for Lapulapu, the chief of Mactan whose warriors defeated Ferdinand Magellan's men and who is honoured as a national hero in the Philippines.
shrunken-skull: The Shrunken Skull is a short mid-century tiki drink of two rums, lime and grenadine, best known from the Mai-Kai in Fort Lauderdale and traditionally served in a skull-shaped ceramic mug, with no creator on record.
port-light: The Port Light is usually credited to Sandro Conti, a bartender at the Kahiki Supper Club in Columbus, Ohio, the grand Polynesian restaurant that opened in 1961. It was served in a red glass shaped like a ship's port light, the source of its name, and its bourbon base makes it an outlier in a category built on rum.
blue-hawaiian: The blue begins in 1957, when a sales representative for the Dutch liqueur house Bols asked Harry Yee, head bartender at the Waikiki resort now called the Hilton Hawaiian Village, to create a drink using blue curaçao. Yee's answer was the Blue Hawaii, made with rum, vodka, curaçao, pineapple and sweet-and-sour. The Blue Hawaiian is a later variation that crosses Yee's idea with the Piña Colada, swapping the sour mix for coconut cream; it has no recorded creator, and menus have used the two names interchangeably ever since.
chi-chi: The Chi Chi is the vodka version of the Piña Colada, with pineapple and coconut cream, tied to the resort bars of mid-century Hawaii, though no one has a documented claim to inventing it.
bahama-breeze: The Bahama Breeze is a Caribbean resort-style mix of coconut rum, banana and pineapple under a float of dark rum, with no recorded creator or date, best treated as a style made a little differently wherever it is served.
rum-barrel: The Rum Barrel is a Don the Beachcomber punch, one of the big drinks Donn Beach built by layering several rums, juices and sweeteners, and other Polynesian restaurants served their own versions, among them the Mai-Kai in Fort Lauderdale, which calls it the Barrel O' Rum.
aku-aku: The Aku Aku takes its name from Aku-Aku, Thor Heyerdahl's bestselling account of his Easter Island expedition, a title tiki culture borrowed freely, and the blended drink of light rum, peach, pineapple, lime and mint has no recorded creator.
sidewinders-fang: The Sidewinder's Fang is a mid-century Polynesian-restaurant riff on Don the Beachcomber's Cobra's Fang, a long punch of Demerara and gold rums with passion fruit, orange, lime and falernum, and no single creator is on record.
molokai-mule: The Molokai Mule is a mid-century tiki drink named for the Hawaiian island of Molokai, and its recipes vary from one source to another, with no creator, bar or date on record.
puka-punch: The Puka Punch is a long, multi-rum tiki punch with passion fruit and honey from the Californian tiki tradition, and no creator or date is on record for it.
tahitian-rum-punch: Tahitian rum punch is a family style rather than a single recipe, rhum with lime and tropical juices sweetened with grenadine and poured long over ice, with no recorded creator or date.
hukilau: The Hukilau is a tiki rum drink with curaçao and passion fruit, named for the Hawaiian community net-fishing tradition, with no creator, bar or date on record.
vicious-virgin: The Vicious Virgin is a short, dry rum drink with falernum and curaçao from Don the Beachcomber's Hollywood bar, and the reason for its name is not recorded.
sharks-tooth: The Shark's Tooth is a long, red, soda-topped Demerara rum drink of the mid-century tiki era, one of several recipes to circulate under that name, with no single recorded creator.
cradle-of-life: The Cradle of Life is a tiki-style rum drink unusual for its use of a whole egg, associated with the Hollywood tiki scene, but no recipe book, menu or bartender is on record as its source.
slippery-nipple: The Slippery Nipple is a layered shooter of sambuca and Irish cream from the era of cheekily named shots, and no creator, bar or date has been credited.
duck-fart: Alaska claims this layered shooter of coffee liqueur, Irish cream and Canadian whisky, and the usual story places its invention at the Peanut Farm, a bar in Anchorage, in the 1980s. That account is widely repeated but thinly documented, and no bartender has been named.
alabama-slammer: The Alabama Slammer, Southern Comfort with amaretto, sloe gin and orange juice, is usually linked to the University of Alabama and the early 1970s, though no one has documented the connection or named a creator.
red-headed-slut: This shooter of Jägermeister, peach schnapps and cranberry juice comes out of American shooter culture, its name a reference to the red colour, and no creator, bar or date is on record.
woo-woo: The Woo Woo is a simple vodka, peach schnapps and cranberry drink from the American peach schnapps boom, served long or as a shot, with no recorded creator and no documented explanation for its name.
purple-hooter: The Purple Hooter is an American vodka shooter coloured with black raspberry liqueur and sharpened with lime, and no creator, bar or date is on record for it.
surfer-on-acid: Surfer on Acid is an American shooter that pairs Jägermeister with coconut rum and pineapple juice, and no creator, bar or date has been recorded.
scooby-snack: The Scooby Snack is a creamy green American shooter of melon liqueur, coconut rum and pineapple, named after the dog treats of the Scooby-Doo cartoons, with no creator or date on record.
liquid-marijuana: Liquid Marijuana is an American novelty shooter named only for its green colour, the old trick of blue curaçao meeting yellow pineapple juice, and no creator or date is on record.
three-wise-men: Three Wise Men is a bar joke rather than a cocktail, one measure each of three whiskies whose labels carry men's names, Jack Daniel's, Jim Beam and Johnnie Walker, and it has no recorded creator or date.
prairie-fire: The Prairie Fire is a two-ingredient American shot of tequila with enough hot sauce to sting, named for the burn, with no creator, bar or date on record.
cement-mixer: The Cement Mixer is an American novelty shooter of Irish cream and lime juice, named for the way the acid curdles the cream almost at once, with no creator or date on record.
chartreuse-bomb: Dropping a shot of green Chartreuse into a glass of dry cider is an American bartenders' ritual rather than a recorded recipe, with no creator or date on record.
lemon-drop-martini: The Lemon Drop was invented in the 1970s by Norman Jay Hobday at Henry Africa's, the saloon he ran in San Francisco's Russian Hill neighbourhood. Henry Africa's is widely credited as the first fern bar, and its sugar-rimmed vodka drink, most likely named after the lemon sweet it resembles, became its most enduring creation. The cocktail-glass Lemon Drop Martini and the later shooter both descend from it.
blue-kamikaze: The Blue Kamikaze is the Kamikaze of vodka, orange liqueur and lime coloured with blue curaçao, a purely visual change, and no creator or date is on record for either version.
tokyo-tea: The Tokyo Tea is a green offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea that keeps the white-spirit base and swaps in melon liqueur, and no creator or date is on record for it.
long-beach-iced-tea: The Long Beach Iced Tea is an offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea that swaps the cola for cranberry juice, giving up the resemblance to iced tea, and no creator or date is on record.
adios-motherfucker: Usually listed on menus as the AMF, this blue offshoot of the Long Island Iced Tea takes its colour from blue curaçao, and no creator, bar or date is on record for it.
irish-car-bomb: Charles Burke Cronin Oat created the drink in 1979 at Wilson's Saloon in Norwich, Connecticut. Two years earlier he had added Irish whiskey to a shot of Irish cream and coffee liqueur and called it the IRA, and when he dropped that shot into a glass of stout the car bomb name followed. The name refers to the violence of the Troubles and is widely considered offensive, especially in Ireland, and many bars now serve the drink as an Irish Slammer.
boilermakers-daughter: The Boilermaker's Daughter is a British pub name for Scotch poured into a glass of bitter ale rather than served alongside it, and no creator, pub or date is on record.
sake-bomb: The sake bomb, a cup of sake dropped into a glass of lager, is a serve of Japanese-themed restaurants rather than a traditional Japanese one, and no creator, bar or date is on record.
flaming-sambuca: Sambuca is the anise liqueur of Lazio, first sold commercially under that name by Luigi Manzi in Civitavecchia, the port near Rome, in the nineteenth century, and serving it with coffee beans, con la mosca or 'with the fly', is an old Italian custom in which three beans are traditional. Setting the glass briefly alight to toast the beans is a later bar flourish whose origin is not recorded.
gin-alexander: The first known Alexander was a gin drink, equal parts gin, crème de cacao and sweet cream, printed by Hugo Ensslin in his Recipes for Mixed Drinks of 1916. Its origin is disputed: the story most often told credits Troy Alexander, a bartender at Rector's in New York, who is said to have made a white drink for a dinner celebrating Phoebe Snow, the railroad advertising heroine in a spotless white dress. Harry Craddock's Savoy Cocktail Book of 1930 printed it in London alongside the brandy version that would eventually claim the name.
golden-cadillac: The Golden Cadillac is credited to Poor Red's Bar-B-Q in El Dorado, California, in 1952. The story goes that a newly engaged couple asked the bartender, Frank Klein, for a drink to match the gold Cadillac they had just bought, and he shook Galliano with white crème de cacao and cream. It became the house drink, and Poor Red's is still known for it.
pink-squirrel: Bryant Sharp is usually credited with creating the Pink Squirrel in the 1940s at Bryant's Cocktail Lounge in Milwaukee, the bar he ran, which still pours it. The drink takes its colour from crème de noyaux, a liqueur flavoured with apricot and peach kernels, shaken with white crème de cacao and cream, and it remains a Wisconsin supper club favourite, sometimes made with ice cream.
pink-lady: The Pink Lady is a pre-Prohibition gin drink coloured with grenadine, and some early recipes add applejack, much like a Jack Rose with gin added. The name is usually linked to The Pink Lady, a Broadway musical hit of 1911, or to its star Hazel Dawn. Later recipes, including the Savoy's, dropped the applejack in favour of gin, grenadine and egg white, and the drink went on to pick up a reputation as a soft, sweet order that its original formula hardly earns.
colorado-bulldog: The Colorado Bulldog is an American cream drink of vodka, coffee liqueur and cream topped with cola, a relative of the White Russian, with no documented link to Colorado and no creator or date on record.
godmother: The Godmother is the vodka partner of the Godfather, a two-ingredient drink of vodka and amaretto over ice, and no creator or date is on record for it.
toasted-almond: The Toasted Almond is an American dessert drink of amaretto, coffee liqueur and cream from the years when amaretto was at its most fashionable, with no creator, bar or date on record.
freddy-fudpucker: The Freddy Fudpucker is the tequila offspring of the Harvey Wallbanger, with Galliano floated on tequila and orange juice, and no creator or date is documented for it.
bay-breeze: The Bay Breeze is the pineapple member of the American breeze family of vodka and cranberry highballs, with no creator or date on record.
madras: The Madras is the orange member of the American breeze family of vodka and cranberry highballs, its name usually explained by the red and orange checks of madras cloth, with no creator or date on record.
angels-tip: The Angel's Tip is a layered after-dinner drink of crème de cacao under a float of cream, finished with a cherry, from the early twentieth-century pousse-café tradition, and no single creator is recorded.
velvet-hammer: The Velvet Hammer is a creamy American after-dinner drink of orange liqueur, crème de cacao and cream whose recipe has never settled, and no creator or date is on record.
bitter-giuseppe: Stephen Cole created the Bitter Giuseppe at The Violet Hour in Chicago in the late 2000s, building a Manhattan-style drink with Cynar, the artichoke amaro, as the base rather than a modifier, stirred with sweet vermouth, lemon and orange bitters. It became one of the most familiar of the low-strength, amaro-led cocktails of its time.
art-of-choke: Kyle Davidson created the Art of Choke at The Violet Hour in Chicago around 2008, splitting the base between white rum and Cynar and adding green Chartreuse, lime, demerara syrup and mint over crushed ice. The name puns on the artichoke behind Cynar, the amaro that carries the drink.
enzoni: Vincenzo Errico created the Enzoni at Milk & Honey in New York in the early 2000s, crossing the Negroni with a gin sour and using muddled green grapes in place of sweet vermouth. The name joins Enzo, short for Vincenzo, to Negroni, and Errico also created the Red Hook, another of the drinks that came out of Milk & Honey in those years.
fitzgerald: Dale DeGroff created the Fitzgerald at the Rainbow Room in New York in the early 1990s, a gin sour given depth by a couple of dashes of Angostura and named for the novelist F. Scott Fitzgerald. It has since travelled to cocktail menus around the world.
water-lily: Richard Boccato created the Water Lily at Little Branch in New York in 2007, the year crème de violette returned to American shelves after decades away. It is an equal-parts sour in the mould of the Corpse Reviver No. 2, with gin, orange liqueur, lemon and violette, and its pale violet colour suits the name.
left-hand: Sam Ross created the Left Hand at Milk & Honey in New York around 2007, adding the then-new Xocolatl Mole bitters from Bittermens to a stirred drink of bourbon, sweet vermouth and Campari that closely resembles the older Boulevardier. Its partner is the Right Hand, a rum version made by his Milk & Honey colleague Michael McIlroy.
conference: Brian Miller created the Conference at Death & Co in New York in the late 2000s by splitting an Old Fashioned four ways, between rye, bourbon, cognac and calvados, seasoned with bitters. It became one of the signature drinks of the bar's early years, after Death & Co opened in the East Village at the end of 2006.
bitter-mai-tai: The Bitter Mai Tai is credited to the New York bartender Jeremy Oertel, who replaced much of the rum in the classic Mai Tai with Campari, keeping a measure of Jamaican rum along with lime, orgeat and orange curaçao. It became one of the defining drinks of bitter tiki, in which an amaro takes the lead role.
ginger-rogers: The modern Ginger Rogers, a long gin drink with mint, lime and ginger ale, is credited to the San Francisco bartender Marco Dionysos and associated above all with Absinthe Brasserie and Bar, where he served it. The ginger explains the dancer's name, though no one recorded who first thought of it.
morgenthaler-amaretto-sour: Jeffrey Morgenthaler, the Portland bartender and writer, published his Amaretto Sour in 2012 in a blog post with a characteristically bold title. His argument was that the Amaretto Sour was not a bad drink but a badly made one, usually built from sour mix. He cut the amaretto back, added cask-strength bourbon for structure, and shook it with fresh lemon and egg white. The recipe spread quickly online and is now widely treated as a modern classic.
whiskey-peach-smash: The Whiskey Peach Smash is a seasonal take on the old whiskey smash, with ripe peach muddled alongside the lemon and mint, and no creator or bar is on record for it.
tantris-sidecar: The Tantris Sidecar is credited to the New York bartender Audrey Saunders, who named it after Tantris, the celebrated Munich restaurant. It builds on the classic cognac Sidecar with green Chartreuse among its additions, layering herbal depth over the original's sweet-and-sour frame, and recipes for it vary.
mezcal-mule: Jim Meehan created the Mezcal Mule at PDT in New York in 2008, building it with passion fruit, cucumber, agave, lime and ginger beer rather than simply swapping spirits in a Moscow Mule. Simpler mezcal-and-ginger-beer versions have since become a bar standard, and many drinkers now know it only in that form.
bee-sting: The Bee Sting is a modern variation on the Bee's Knees, the gin, honey and lemon sour, with chilli added for heat, and no creator or date is on record for it.
japanese-highball: Japan's whisky highball took hold in the 1950s, when Suntory opened a chain of Torys bars across the country, serving its affordable Torys whisky with soda. The highball remained central to Japanese drinking until whisky fell out of fashion in the 1980s. In 2008 Suntory launched a campaign to revive it around Kakubin, its square-bottled blend, and the precise, ritualised serve that followed became famous far beyond Japan.
mizuwari: Mizuwari, literally 'cut with water', is the Japanese custom of lengthening whisky with cold still water over ice to drink with food, a national habit rather than an invention, with no single creator.
oyuwari: Oyuwari, shochu cut with hot water, is a traditional winter way of drinking shochu in Kyushu, a regional custom rather than an invention, with no creator or date on record.
chuhai: Chuhai is a contraction of 'shochu highball', the habit of lengthening shochu with soda and fruit flavouring that is usually traced to the izakaya of postwar Tokyo, where shochu was cheaper than whisky or beer. It became a national phenomenon once Takara launched the first canned chuhai, and ready-to-drink versions now fill convenience-store fridges across Japan in dozens of flavours. No single creator is recorded.
denki-bran: Denki Bran is usually dated to 1882, though accounts of the exact year differ. Its creator, Kamiya Denbei, had opened a liquor shop in Asakusa, Tokyo, and in 1912 the premises became Kamiya Bar, which still serves the drink. In the Meiji era electricity stood for everything modern, and new goods were often sold as 'electric', so Kamiya's brandy-based blend became Electric Brandy; its exact recipe remains a secret.
hoppy: Hoppy went on sale in Tokyo in 1948 as a beer-flavoured soft drink, at a time when real beer was expensive and hard to find. Drinkers soon found that it made cheap shochu taste like beer, and the pairing became a Tokyo izakaya fixture that postwar nostalgia has kept alive.
yuzu-sour: The yuzu sour is a fresh-citrus member of Japan's izakaya sour family, shochu and soda with the juice of yuzu and a little honey, and no single creator or date is on record.
calpis-sour: Calpis, the cultured-milk cordial at the heart of this drink, was launched in Japan by Kaiun Mishima in the Taisho era, after he had encountered airag, fermented mare's milk, while travelling in Mongolia. The name joins cal, from calcium, to pis, from sarpis, a Sanskrit word from Buddhist teaching, chosen after consulting the composer Kosaku Yamada among others. Mixed with shochu and soda, Calpis became a staple sour of the izakaya, though no one claims the first glass.
sakerinha: The Sakerinha swaps the cachaça of Brazil's Caipirinha for sake, keeping the muddled lime and sugar, and it has no recorded creator or date.
baijiu-sour: The Baijiu Sour gives China's grain spirit the classic sour treatment, shaken with lemon, honey and egg white, and it has many authors and no single recorded creator or date.
cynar-spritz: The spritz is usually traced to the Habsburg years in the Veneto, when soldiers and merchants from the north are said to have asked for a splash of water to soften the local wine; bitter liqueurs and prosecco came later. Cynar, the artichoke-based amaro made from thirteen herbs and plants, was launched after the Second World War by the Venetian entrepreneur Angelo Dalle Molle, and swapping it for Aperol or Select gives a darker, more bitter spritz now familiar in the bars of the Veneto.
select-spritz: Select was created in Venice in 1920 by the brothers Mario and Vittorio Pilla, and it became the city's own bitter for the spritz. The spritz itself is usually traced to the Habsburg years in the Veneto, when visitors from the north are said to have asked for a splash of water to soften the local wine; bitter liqueurs and prosecco came later. In Venice's bacari, the city's small wine bars, many still regard Select as the proper base for a spritz veneziano.
puccini: The Puccini is usually credited to Harry's Bar in Venice, where Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini, white peach purée with prosecco, and named it after a Venetian painter. The bar went on to pair sparkling wine with other seasonal fruits and other artists: strawberry for the Rossini, pomegranate for the Tintoretto, and fresh mandarin juice for the Puccini, named after the composer of La Bohème and Tosca.
tintoretto: The Tintoretto belongs to the family of fruit-and-sparkling-wine drinks that grew up at Harry's Bar in Venice after Giuseppe Cipriani created the Bellini and named it for the Venetian painter Giovanni Bellini. The bar paired other fruits with other artists, and pomegranate went to Tintoretto, the Venetian master whose vast canvases cover the walls and ceilings of the Scuola Grande di San Rocco. It is mixed with prosecco and served in the colder months, when pomegranates are in season.
carajillo-43: The carajillo, black coffee laced with spirit, is an old Spanish café habit, and the stories told about its name are disputed. Mexico remade it around Licor 43, the vanilla-and-citrus liqueur from Cartagena, Spain, named for its forty-three ingredients, shaking it over ice with espresso, and the Carajillo 43 became a fixture of Mexican restaurants and after-dinner tables. No single creator is recorded.
mastiha-spritz: The Mastiha Spritz is a modern serve that lengthens mastiha, the pine-scented Greek liqueur made from the mastic resin of southern Chios, with soda, lemon and prosecco, and it has no recorded creator or date.
herrengedeck: The Herrengedeck, literally the gentlemen's set, is a Berlin bar custom of serving a pilsner alongside a glass of sekt, a corner-bar tradition rather than an invention, with no recorded creator or date.
cubanito: The Cubanito is the rum-based Cuban member of the Bloody Mary family, white rum with tomato, lime and spice, and no creator, bar or date is documented for it.
grzaniec: Grzaniec, from the Polish word for warming, is the mulled beer or wine of Polish winters, spiced with honey, cloves, ginger and cinnamon, a folk tradition with no recorded creator or date.
almdudler-spritzer: Almdudler, the herbal soda in this spritzer, was created in Vienna by Erwin Klein, who launched it in the late fifties after three years of development and took the name from the old Alpine expression auf der Alm dudeln, roughly to yodel on the mountain pasture. In the wine regions of Lower Austria and Burgenland it became a popular mixer for local red and white wines, and the spritzer that results is a household serve rather than an invention, with no single creator.
dutch-mule: The Dutch Mule hands the mule format of ginger beer and lime to jenever, the malt-wine spirit of the Netherlands and Belgium, and no creator or date is recorded for it.
irish-mule: The Irish Mule applies the mule formula of ginger beer and lime to Irish whiskey, one of many regional versions of the Moscow Mule, with no creator or date on record.
sima: Sima is Finland's traditional drink for Vappu, the May Day festival: a lightly fermented lemonade bottled for a few days with raisins, which rise to the surface when it is ready. Older recipes used honey, which is why sima is often described as a mead, though most households now make it with sugar. It is a folk tradition with no single creator, made in homes across the country each spring.
medovukha: Medovukha is the honey drink of the East Slavs, mentioned in medieval chronicles long before distilling reached the region and made by fermenting honey with water and spices. Its name comes from med, the Slavic word for honey. Over the centuries it ranged from long-aged honey drinks to quicker boiled versions, and today it is made both at home and commercially, notably around the old town of Suzdal. It is a folk tradition rather than an invention.
uvita: The most famous uvita in Uruguay is the house drink of Bar Fun Fun, a nineteenth-century Montevideo bar long tied to the city's tango history, which pours its sweet, wine-based uvita in small glasses from a recipe it keeps to itself. Uvita simply means 'little grape', and the name is also used more loosely for home-made sweet wine drinks with no single creator.
islenskur-kaffi: Icelandic coffee is a café and home serve of strong coffee with a measure of brennivín, the caraway-flavoured spirit of Iceland, topped with cream in the manner of Irish coffee, with no creator or date on record.
ca-phe-trung-rum: Hanoi's egg coffee, the base of this drink, is usually credited to Nguyen Van Giang, a bartender at the Metropole hotel, who whipped egg yolk with sugar and condensed milk as a stand-in for fresh milk during a milk shortage in the late forties. He later opened his own café, Cafe Giang, which his family still runs and where the coffee is served in cups set in hot water to keep it warm. Stirring in dark rum is a modern bar addition, with no recorded creator.
nam-manao-soda: Nam manao soda, fresh lime juice with sugar, a pinch of salt and soda water, is an everyday Thai street drink, and the version lengthened with Thai rum has no recorded creator or date.
palm-wine-punch: Palm Wine Punch lengthens West African palm wine, the fermented sap of the palm, with gin, ginger, lime and honey, a modern party style of Nigeria's cities with no recorded creator or date.
tej-spritz: The Tej Spritz is a modern serve that lengthens tej, the Ethiopian honey wine bittered with gesho leaves, with soda and lemon, and it has no recorded creator or date.
ceylon-arrack-sour: The Ceylon Arrack Sour gives Sri Lanka's coconut-sap spirit the classic sour treatment, sweetened with jaggery, a modern serve of Colombo's bars with no recorded creator or date.
chacha-sour: The Chacha Sour treats Georgia's grape spirit as a sour with lemon and honey and adds tarragon, a defining Georgian flavour, as a modern serve of Tbilisi's bars with no recorded creator or date.
moroccan-mint-cooler: The Moroccan Mint Cooler is a contemporary bar serve that chills sweet Moroccan mint tea and adds boukha, the fig spirit of neighbouring Tunisia, and no creator or date is on record.
masala-chai-toddy: The Masala Chai Toddy stirs dark rum into Indian masala chai, black tea boiled with milk and spices such as cardamom and ginger, a modern winter serve with no recorded creator or date.
caju-amigo: Caju Amigo, friendly cashew, is a northeastern Brazilian pairing of cachaça with the juice of the cashew apple, a bar custom rather than a recorded invention, with no creator or date on record.
vermut-torrontes: The Vermut Torrontés is a modern Argentine serve of local vermouth over ice with soda and orange in the manner of the Buenos Aires vermú hour, its name pointing to the aromatic white Torrontés grape, and no creator or date is on record.
averna: In 1868 Salvatore Averna, a Caltanissetta justice of the peace from a family of drapers, began producing an amaro for guests at his home, using a herbal infusion whose recipe Fra Girolamo, prior of the Abbey of Santo Spirito, had given him in 1859 as a token of gratitude. His son Francesco built the family business, King Umberto I honoured him for the amaro in 1895, and in 1912 the company was authorised to carry the royal crest on its labels.
amaro-montenegro: Stanislao Cobianchi created this Bologna amaro in 1885 and first sold it as Elisir Lungavita. In 1896 he renamed it Amaro Montenegro in honour of Princess Elena of Montenegro, who married Crown Prince Victor Emmanuel, later King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, that year. Its proprietary blend of forty botanicals includes orange peel, vanilla and eucalyptus, and it is still produced near Bologna, at San Lazzaro di Savena.
ramazzotti: Ausano Ramazzotti created his amaro in Milan in 1815, macerating at least thirty-three roots and herbs, and it is often described as the first Italian aperitif not based on wine. In 1848 he opened a bar on Via Santa Margherita, a few steps from La Scala, where it could be served by the glass to the city's theatregoers. Pernod Ricard acquired the company in 1985, and production moved from Lainate to Canelli in Piedmont in 1994.
braulio: Braulio has been made in Bormio, in the Valtellina, since 1875, from a recipe of alpine herbs, roots and berries credited to the local pharmacist Francesco Peloni. It takes its name from Monte Braulio and the Braulio valley above the town, where its herbs were traditionally gathered, and it is still produced and aged in oak casks in Bormio.
amaro-nonino: The Nonino family has distilled in Friuli since 1897, when Orazio Nonino set up a still at Ronchi di Percoto. The firm's turning point came in 1973, when Benito and Giannola Nonino released the first commercial grappa made from a single grape variety, Picolit, a move that helped lift grappa's reputation across Italy. Their amaro, Quintessentia, is built on aged grappa rather than neutral spirit, and its role in Sam Ross's Paper Plane made it a bartender's staple far beyond Italy.
meletti: The Meletti firm of Ascoli Piceno dates from 1870, when Silvio Meletti began producing anisetta, the anise liqueur for which the family is still best known in the Marche. The company's amaro followed, with a blend that includes saffron and violet, and Caffè Meletti, the family's café on Ascoli's Piazza del Popolo, became one of the historic cafés of central Italy. Locals still take the anisetta in their coffee.
sfumato-rabarbaro: Sfumato Rabarbaro comes from Cappelletti, a long-established family distillery in Aldeno, in Trentino. It belongs to the rabarbaro family of Italian amari built on rhubarb root, and the smoky character of its Chinese rhubarb gives it its name: sfumato means smoky, and is also the painter's term for soft, hazy shading.
cardamaro: Cardamaro is made in Canelli, in the Asti wine country of Piedmont, by the long-established Bosca family firm. It is a vino amaro, a bitter built on wine rather than spirit, flavoured with cardoon and blessed thistle and rested in oak. Cardoon is a thistle and a close relative of the artichoke, which puts Cardamaro in the same botanical family as Cynar, though the two taste quite different.
amaro-lucano: Pasquale Vena, a pastry chef, created Amaro Lucano in 1894 in Pisticci, in Basilicata, blending more than thirty herbs, and the name comes from Lucania, the ancient name for the region. By around 1900 the Vena family had become official suppliers to the House of Savoy. After the Second World War his sons Leonardo and Giuseppe turned the workshop into a factory, and production later moved to a new plant at Pisticci Scalo.
